    How this is measured

    A player's rating says how they'd fare against the average tour player of the whole period — 0 is that average. Serve and return are rated separately. Hard, clay and grass are weighted by how much of the tour is played on each (hard 55%, clay 33%, grass 12%). Surface ratings use career results, and small samples stay closer to a player's overall level.

    Runs marked results only are from before 1991, when only match results exist: they use a match-level rating anchored to each era's No. 11–50 player. Judge them against each other rather than against the point-model runs.
    How this is measured

    Every tour title since 1968, judged three ways: how tough the draw was, how big a favourite the champion was going in, and how well he actually played once there. The draw score belongs to the tournament; the other two belong to the player.

    1 · Draw
    How tough was the path?

    We send a fixed yardstick player — the average world No. 3–7 of 2000–25 — through the champion's exact draw: the same opponents, at their level that quarter, on that surface. His chance of winning the whole thing is the draw score. Every score is ranked against other draws at the same level of event, so the words are relative to the level: brutal means a brutal path for a Slam — tougher than 85% of slam draws — or a brutal path for a 250/500, tougher than 85% of 250/500 draws.

    2 · Favourite
    How likely was he to win it?

    The champion's own chance of winning that same draw, from his rating going in. Around 60% means he was the man to beat; under 10% means almost nobody saw it coming. "Going in" means his rating at the end of the previous calendar quarter, so a hot streak in the weeks just before the event (a clay swing before Roland Garros) isn't counted yet, and an in-form champion can look more surprising than he was. For a beaten finalist it's his chance of winning the title, final included.

    3 · Performance
    How well did he play?

    How far above his going-in level he won points through the run, plus the sets and games he dropped. Champions nearly always play above themselves, so the label is a percentile among champions at the same level of event — dominant means better than 80% of them, not an absolute standard.

    How this is measured

    Six measured components on one scale. Titles count only through Hardware, and only after weighting each by how hard it was to win. Move the weights; the list, the scores and the rank intervals recompute live. The default weights are one defensible opinion, not a verdict.

    Peak and sustained excellence are Elo-like ratings from the point model (1991→) or, before that, the results-only model mapped onto the same axis with its extra uncertainty (results only and mixed careers). Hardware is every tour title in "standard slams": a typical Masters is worth about half a slam and a typical 250 about a seventh, then each title is nudged by how tough its draw was — never below half or above double its level's usual worth, so no single brutal draw can count like a career.

    Built from the tennis data warehouse — 95,000 tour matches with serve points (1991–2026, 15M points) and every Open Era result behind them. Ratings adjust for opponent, surface and court speed; simulated matches are played point → game → set → match.
